title: Spatial data analysis: week 9 tutorial
text:
Week 9 — Areal data and Moran’s I
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
We analyse the Lip cancer data in scotland. The data contain, for each of the Scotland counties, the number of observed and expected lip cancer cases among males in Scotland between 1975-1980, and a variable that indicates the proportion of the population engaged in agriculture, fishing, or forestry (aff). The aff variable is related to exposure to sunlight which is a risk factor for lip cancer. The data also contain the shapefile of the Scotland counties and everything can be found in scotland_lip

title: Install R packages
text: Everything this course uses is bundled in one package, lsda. Installing it brings the datasets, the helper functions and the interactive apps.

title: Install R packages
text:
Install
install.packages("lsda", repos = c("https://olatunjijohnson.r-universe.dev",
                                   "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
The r-universe repository serves pre-built binaries, so you do not need a compiler. If that repository is unavailable, install from source instead:
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("olatunjijohnson/lsda")

Check it worked
library(lsda)
data(cattle)
dim(cattle)          # 60 x 12
run_app()            # lists the interactive apps

title: Install R packages
text:
If something goes wrong
Spatial packages (sf, spdep, terra) need system libraries GDAL, GEOS and PROJ. On the University machines these are already present. On your own Linux machine:
sudo apt install libgdal-dev libgeos-dev libproj-dev libudunits2-dev
On macOS with Homebrew:
brew install gdal geos proj udunits
Windows binaries bundle these already, so no extra step is needed.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis: week 1 tutorial
text:
Week 1 — Exploring longitudinal data






NoteHow to use this page





Each exercise below is a live R session. Type your answer and press Run; you can experiment freely, nothing is saved and nothing can break. The first block takes a few seconds to start while R loads in your browser.
Worked solutions are on Canvas.



























Q1: This question relates to the cattle data, available in the course package as cattle.









Consult the R online manuals, specifically “An Introduction to R” (PDF file), Section 7, titled “Reading Data from Files.” Proceed to import the dataset into R.










Generate a spaghetti plot for the cattle data.










Calculate the sample means for observations at each time point. Additionally, compute the sample covariance matrix and sample correlation matrix.










Create a pairwise scatter plot for the cattle data. Analyse and describe the key features of the observed correlations.










Divide the cattle dataset into two groups, Group A and Group B. For each group, determine the sample means at each time point, as well as the sample covariance and sample correlation.










Produce pairwise scatter plots for each group. Identify and discuss any similarities or differences between the two groups evident in the plots.










Plot the sample means of both groups against time within a single figure. Provide your interpretations and conclusions drawn from the figure.









Q2 You will work with longitudinal data on lung function growth in school-age girls from Topeka, Kansas, as part of the Six Cities Study of Air Pollution and Health. The dataset contains repeated pulmonary function measurements from 299 girls, typically enrolled around ages 6-10 and followed annually until high school graduation or loss to follow-up. The number of observations per individual ranges from 1 to 12, making the dataset unbalanced with respect to age.
At each visit, lung function was measured using simple spirometry, and the outcome of interest is the logarithm of the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) to height, i.e., log(FEV1/height).
The dataset is available in the course package.
Key variables include:
- id: unique identifier for each girl
- ht: height (m)
- age: age at measurement (years)
- baseht: height at the first visit
- baseage: age at the first visit
- fev1: volume of air exhaled in the first second (litres)
- logfev1: logarithm of fev1
- logfev1_ht: pre-computed log(fev1/height)
  









Load the dataset and check the structure of the data. How many observations are there in total? How many individuals?










Summarise the number of observations per individual. What does this tell you about the balance of the data?










Produce a plot of log(fev1 / height) against age for 50 randomly selected girls. Connect points for the same individual. Comment on the variability between individuals and the measurement patterns over age.










Compute and plot the average log(fev1 / height) at each age, aggregating across individuals.

title: Longitudinal data analysis: week 5 tutorial
text:
Week 5 — Generalised estimating equations






NoteHow to use this page





Each exercise below is a live R session. Type your answer and press Run; you can experiment freely, nothing is saved and nothing can break. The first block takes a few seconds to start while R loads in your browser.
Worked solutions are on Canvas.



























In a study of the effects of vitamin A deficiency in preschool children (available in the course package as ichs), 250 children were examined at an initial clinic visit and again at 3 month intervals for a year (at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 months after the first visit). The investigators are particularly interested in assessing whether or not the children with vitamin A deficiency are at increased risk of developing respiratory infection. At each examination, the presence or absence of respiratory infection, the child’s age in years, gender, and whether they suffered from vitamin A deficiency are recorded. The ICHS data file has the following columns:

Let \(Y_i\) be the vector of responses for the \(i\)th child, consisting of the elements \(Y_{ij}\), which are observations on whether the child has a respiratory infection at time \(t_{ij}\) (recorded in months; Yes=1 and No=0). Write down a model for \(E(Y_{ij})\) with an appropriate link function that is linear in an intercept and additive terms for time, age, gender, and vitamin A status. Also, write down \(\mbox{Var}(Y_{ij})\) given the nature of the response.










Fit the model in part (1) without taking the within-subject correlation into account, i.e., taking all the observations from the children as if they were independent. Based on this fit, is there any sufficient evidence to suggest that the mean pattern of respiratory response is associated with the presence or absence of vitamin A deficiency? State the null hypothesis corresponding to this question in your model (a), describe the test statistic and p-value on which you draw the conclusion, and state your conclusion.










Write down a model that extends the model in part (1) by taking into account the within-subject correlation among repeated measurements.










Fit your model in part (3) to the data. Assuming that your model for the within-subject correlation is correct, conduct a hypothesis test for the null hypothesis in part (2). State your conclusion. Does the result agree with that in part (2)? Based on the results from your R output, give an explanation for your conclusion. Provide a summary of your model selection and justify your choice.










Is there any sufficient evidence to suggest that the probability of respiratory infection changes over the 15 month study period? Is there any sufficient evidence to suggest that it is worthwhile to take gender into account in understanding the risk of respiratory infection in this population of children?

title: Spatial data analysis: week 8 tutorial
text:
Challenge
Use the Liberia data from the RiskMap package to build a binomial geostatistical model to investigate the relationship between log elevation and onchocerciasis prevalence in Liberia.. The dataset can be called in R using data(liberia). This data-set contains counts of reported onchocerciasis (or riverblindess) cases from 91 villages sampled across Liberia. The variables are as follows:

lat latitude of the of sampled villages.
long longitude of the sampled villages.
ntest number of tested people for the presence nodules.
npos number of people that tested positive for the presence of nodules.
elevation the elevation in meters of the sampled village.
log_elevation the log-transformed elevation in meters of the sampled village.
